data.name: VisaoGeral.Title
data.value: Overview

data.name: VisaoGeral.Block01
data.value: Kubernetes runs and manages containerized applications declaratively. You describe the desired state; Kubernetes controllers observe the actual state and work to make it converge. Keep two ideas separate: hierarchy describes ownership and composition; relationships describe resources that select, reference, or control other resources.

data.name: VisaoGeral.Group
data.value: Groups.Foundations

data.name: Cluster.Title
data.value: Cluster

data.name: Cluster.Block01
data.value: A cluster is the complete Kubernetes environment: its control plane, worker nodes, namespaces, workloads, networking, storage, policies, and configuration. It is the context in which Kubernetes resources exist.

data.name: Cluster.Group
data.value: Groups.Foundations

data.name: ControlPlane.Title
data.value: Control plane

data.name: ControlPlane.Block01
data.value: The control plane manages the cluster. Its main components are the API server, etcd, scheduler, and controller manager. The API server is the entry point for clients; etcd stores cluster state; the scheduler assigns Pods to nodes; controllers keep observed state close to desired state.

data.name: ControlPlane.Group
data.value: Groups.Foundations

data.name: WorkerNode.Title
data.value: Worker node

data.name: WorkerNode.Block01
data.value: A Node is a physical or virtual machine that runs workloads. The kubelet communicates with the API server, the container runtime runs containers, and networking components route traffic. A Pod is scheduled onto a Node, but it should not be treated as permanently bound to that machine.

data.name: WorkerNode.Group
data.value: Groups.Foundations

data.name: Namespace.Title
data.value: Namespace

data.name: Namespace.Block01
data.value: A Namespace logically partitions namespaced resources inside a cluster. Teams often use namespaces to separate environments, apply policies, and set quotas. A Namespace is not a machine or virtual machine; one Node can run Pods from several namespaces.

data.name: Namespace.Group
data.value: Groups.Foundations

data.name: Workloads.Title
data.value: Workloads

data.name: Workloads.Block01
data.value: A workload is an application or process Kubernetes must run. Common workload resources are Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, and CronJob. Each expresses a different lifecycle and scheduling model.

data.name: Workloads.Group
data.value: Groups.Workloads

data.name: Deployment.Title
data.value: Deployment

data.name: Deployment.Block01
data.value: A Deployment manages stateless applications. It declares the desired replica count and Pod template, then creates and updates ReplicaSets. A rolling update replaces Pods gradually while the controller works toward the declared state.

data.name: Deployment.Group
data.value: Groups.Workloads

data.name: Replicaset.Title
data.value: ReplicaSet

data.name: Replicaset.Block01
data.value: A ReplicaSet keeps a requested number of matching Pods running. Deployments normally manage ReplicaSets, so applications are usually changed through a Deployment rather than by editing its ReplicaSet directly.

data.name: Replicaset.Group
data.value: Groups.Workloads

data.name: Pod.Title
data.value: Pod

data.name: Pod.Block01
data.value: A Pod is Kubernetes' smallest deployable unit. It contains one or more containers that share a network identity and can share volumes. Most Pods have one main application container; sidecars are also common. A Pod is scheduled and replaced as a unit.

data.name: Pod.Group
data.value: Groups.Workloads

data.name: Containers.Title
data.value: Containers

data.name: Containers.Block01
data.value: A container is a process running inside a Pod. Kubernetes schedules Pods, not individual containers. Containers in one Pod share the Pod network and may mount the same volumes.

data.name: Containers.Group
data.value: Groups.Workloads

data.name: LabelsESelectors.Title
data.value: Labels and selectors

data.name: LabelsESelectors.Block01
data.value: Labels are key/value metadata attached to objects. Selectors choose objects whose labels match a rule. A label shared by two resources does not itself create a Kubernetes dependency; a resource such as a Service or Deployment must use a matching selector for the label to affect behavior.

data.name: LabelsESelectors.Group
data.value: Groups.Networking

data.name: Service.Title
data.value: Service

data.name: Service.Block01
data.value: Pod addresses can change when Pods are replaced. A Service gives clients a stable address and selects backend Pods by labels. Common types are ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, and ExternalName. The selector-to-Pod association is distinct from ownership.

data.name: Service.Group
data.value: Groups.Networking

data.name: IngressEGatewayApi.Title
data.value: Ingress and Gateway API

data.name: IngressEGatewayApi.Block01
data.value: Ingress and Gateway API describe HTTP/HTTPS entry points and route traffic to Services. Ingress is the older, simpler API. Gateway API offers richer role separation and routing features. Neither replaces the Service that provides a stable backend.

data.name: IngressEGatewayApi.Group
data.value: Groups.Networking

data.name: Configmap.Title
data.value: ConfigMap

data.name: Configmap.Block01
data.value: A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration. Pods can consume its keys as environment variables or mounted files. Do not store passwords, tokens, or private keys in a ConfigMap.

data.name: Configmap.Group
data.value: Groups.Configuration

data.name: Secret.Title
data.value: Secret

data.name: Secret.Block01
data.value: A Secret represents sensitive values such as passwords, tokens, certificates, and connection strings. Base64 encoding in the API representation is not encryption. Protection depends on RBAC, transport security, and the cluster's storage encryption configuration. This app hides Secret values by default and only requests them after an explicit reveal action.

data.name: Secret.Group
data.value: Groups.Configuration

data.name: Storage.Title
data.value: Storage

data.name: Storage.Block01
data.value: Persistent storage separates data lifetime from Pod lifetime. A Pod can request storage through a PersistentVolumeClaim; the claim can bind to a PersistentVolume, which represents capacity made available to the cluster.

data.name: Storage.Group
data.value: Groups.Configuration

data.name: Persistentvolumeclaim.Title
data.value: PersistentVolumeClaim

data.name: Persistentvolumeclaim.Block01
data.value: A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is an application's request for storage capacity and access modes. A Pod mounts the claim instead of depending on a specific storage device.

data.name: Persistentvolumeclaim.Group
data.value: Groups.Configuration

data.name: Persistentvolume.Title
data.value: PersistentVolume

data.name: Persistentvolume.Block01
data.value: A PersistentVolume (PV) represents storage capacity in the cluster. It may be provisioned in advance or dynamically for a claim. Its implementation connects Kubernetes to a storage backend.

data.name: Persistentvolume.Group
data.value: Groups.Configuration

data.name: Storageclass.Title
data.value: StorageClass

data.name: Storageclass.Block01
data.value: A StorageClass describes a class of dynamically provisioned storage. A PVC can name a class; a provisioner then creates a matching PV according to that class's parameters and policies.

data.name: Storageclass.Group
data.value: Groups.Configuration

data.name: Statefulset.Title
data.value: StatefulSet

data.name: Statefulset.Block01
data.value: A StatefulSet manages Pods that need stable identities or storage associated with each replica. Names such as database-0 and database-1 remain predictable across replacement. Stateful workloads often need ordered startup and shutdown.

data.name: Statefulset.Group
data.value: Groups.Stateful

data.name: Daemonset.Title
data.value: DaemonSet

data.name: Daemonset.Block01
data.value: A DaemonSet schedules a Pod onto every eligible Node, or onto Nodes matching its scheduling rules. Typical uses include logging, monitoring, networking, and security agents.

data.name: Daemonset.Group
data.value: Groups.Stateful

data.name: JobECronjob.Title
data.value: Job and CronJob

data.name: JobECronjob.Block01
data.value: A Job runs work that should complete, such as a migration or batch task. A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule. Jobs and their Pods remain separate resources, connected through ownership.

data.name: JobECronjob.Group
data.value: Groups.Stateful

data.name: RequestsELimits.Title
data.value: Requests and limits

data.name: RequestsELimits.Block01
data.value: Requests describe the CPU and memory a container asks the scheduler to reserve. Limits cap the resources it may consume. Requests affect placement; limits affect runtime enforcement.

data.name: RequestsELimits.Group
data.value: Groups.Stateful

data.name: Scheduling.Title
data.value: Scheduling

data.name: Scheduling.Block01
data.value: The scheduler chooses a Node for each unscheduled Pod. It considers resource requests, node availability, affinity rules, taints and tolerations, topology constraints, and other policies. A Pod can remain Pending when no eligible Node is available.

data.name: Scheduling.Group
data.value: Groups.Scheduling

data.name: NodeAffinity.Title
data.value: Node affinity

data.name: NodeAffinity.Block01
data.value: Node affinity expresses required or preferred Node labels for a Pod. Required rules constrain placement; preferred rules guide the scheduler without making a matching Node mandatory.

data.name: NodeAffinity.Group
data.value: Groups.Scheduling

data.name: PodAntiAffinity.Title
data.value: Pod anti-affinity

data.name: PodAntiAffinity.Block01
data.value: Pod anti-affinity can keep related Pods apart, for example by spreading replicas across Nodes. This can reduce the effect of a single machine failure, subject to available capacity and topology rules.

data.name: PodAntiAffinity.Group
data.value: Groups.Scheduling

data.name: TaintsETolerations.Title
data.value: Taints and tolerations

data.name: TaintsETolerations.Block01
data.value: A taint marks a Node so that Pods without a matching toleration are not scheduled there, or may be evicted. A toleration allows a Pod to be considered; it does not by itself force placement on that Node.

data.name: TaintsETolerations.Group
data.value: Groups.Scheduling

data.name: TopologySpreadConstraints.Title
data.value: Topology spread constraints

data.name: TopologySpreadConstraints.Block01
data.value: Topology spread constraints distribute Pods across failure domains such as Nodes or zones. They help avoid concentrating all replicas in one domain, subject to the configured skew and scheduling constraints.

data.name: TopologySpreadConstraints.Group
data.value: Groups.Scheduling

data.name: HealthProbes.Title
data.value: Health probes

data.name: HealthProbes.Block01
data.value: Startup probes allow slow applications time to initialize. Readiness probes determine whether a container should receive traffic. Liveness probes detect a process that should be restarted. These probes answer different questions and should be configured for the application's behavior.

data.name: HealthProbes.Group
data.value: Groups.Availability

data.name: HorizontalPodAutoscalerHpa.Title
data.value: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler

data.name: HorizontalPodAutoscalerHpa.Block01
data.value: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) adjusts a workload's replica count using resource or custom metrics. It needs usable metrics and a scalable target. It adds or removes Pods; it does not resize the resources allocated to each Pod.

data.name: HorizontalPodAutoscalerHpa.Group
data.value: Groups.Availability

data.name: VerticalPodAutoscalerVpa.Title
data.value: Vertical Pod Autoscaler

data.name: VerticalPodAutoscalerVpa.Block01
data.value: The Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) recommends or adjusts CPU and memory requests for Pods. Depending on its mode, applying a recommendation can require Pod replacement. HPA changes the number of Pods; VPA changes per-Pod resource sizing.

data.name: VerticalPodAutoscalerVpa.Group
data.value: Groups.Availability

data.name: PoddisruptionbudgetPdb.Title
data.value: PodDisruptionBudget

data.name: PoddisruptionbudgetPdb.Block01
data.value: A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) limits voluntary disruptions so a minimum number or percentage of selected Pods remains available. It affects operations such as draining a Node; it does not prevent involuntary failures.

data.name: PoddisruptionbudgetPdb.Group
data.value: Groups.Availability

data.name: Priorityclass.Title
data.value: PriorityClass

data.name: Priorityclass.Block01
data.value: A PriorityClass assigns relative scheduling priority to Pods. When resources are scarce, higher-priority Pods may be scheduled before lower-priority Pods, and preemption may remove lower-priority workloads when allowed.

data.name: Priorityclass.Group
data.value: Groups.Availability

data.name: Serviceaccount.Title
data.value: ServiceAccount

data.name: Serviceaccount.Block01
data.value: A ServiceAccount is an identity that a Pod can use when calling the Kubernetes API. Its effective permissions come from authorization rules such as RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings, not from the ServiceAccount object alone.

data.name: Serviceaccount.Group
data.value: Groups.Security

data.name: Rbac.Title
data.value: RBAC

data.name: Rbac.Block01
data.value: Role-based access control (RBAC) grants verbs such as get, list, watch, create, patch, and delete on specified resources and scopes. Roles and RoleBindings are namespace-scoped; ClusterRoles and ClusterRoleBindings can grant cluster-wide permissions.

data.name: Rbac.Group
data.value: Groups.Security

data.name: Securitycontext.Title
data.value: SecurityContext

data.name: Securitycontext.Block01
data.value: A SecurityContext configures process and container security, including user and group IDs, Linux capabilities, privilege escalation, and read-only filesystems. Pod-level and container-level settings can have different scope.

data.name: Securitycontext.Group
data.value: Groups.Security

data.name: Networkpolicy.Title
data.value: NetworkPolicy

data.name: Networkpolicy.Block01
data.value: A NetworkPolicy selects Pods and describes allowed ingress or egress traffic. Enforcement depends on a network plugin that supports NetworkPolicy. Policies are additive, and their effect depends on the selected Pods and namespace.

data.name: Networkpolicy.Group
data.value: Groups.Security

data.name: Resourcequota.Title
data.value: ResourceQuota

data.name: Resourcequota.Block01
data.value: A ResourceQuota limits aggregate resource consumption or object counts within a Namespace. It can constrain CPU, memory, storage, and the number of selected resource types.

data.name: Resourcequota.Group
data.value: Groups.Security

data.name: Limitrange.Title
data.value: LimitRange

data.name: Limitrange.Block01
data.value: A LimitRange sets per-object minimums, maximums, or defaults for resources in a Namespace. ResourceQuota limits the namespace total; LimitRange governs individual Pods, containers, or claims.

data.name: Limitrange.Group
data.value: Groups.Security

data.name: CrdCustomResourceDefinition.Title
data.value: CustomResourceDefinition

data.name: CrdCustomResourceDefinition.Block01
data.value: A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) adds a new kind to the Kubernetes API. Once installed, users can create custom resources that follow the CRD schema. A CRD defines a type; an operator or controller usually implements its behavior.

data.name: CrdCustomResourceDefinition.Group
data.value: Groups.Operations

data.name: Controller.Title
data.value: Controller

data.name: Controller.Block01
data.value: A controller watches API objects and repeatedly compares desired state with observed state. It takes actions to reduce the difference. Controllers are the mechanism behind Deployments, StatefulSets, and many other Kubernetes features.

data.name: Controller.Group
data.value: Groups.Operations

data.name: Operator.Title
data.value: Operator

data.name: Operator.Block01
data.value: An Operator combines CRDs and controllers with application-specific operational knowledge. It can automate tasks such as provisioning, backup, recovery, replication, and upgrades for a particular system.

data.name: Operator.Group
data.value: Groups.Operations

data.name: AdmissionControllers.Title
data.value: Admission controllers

data.name: AdmissionControllers.Block01
data.value: Admission controllers inspect API requests after authentication and authorization but before persistence. They can validate, mutate, or reject objects. They are commonly used to enforce policy and set safe defaults.

data.name: AdmissionControllers.Group
data.value: Groups.Operations

data.name: Helm.Title
data.value: Helm

data.name: Helm.Block01
data.value: Helm packages Kubernetes manifests into Charts with templates and configurable values. It manages releases and rendered resources; it does not replace Kubernetes controllers or guarantee that an application is healthy.

data.name: Helm.Group
data.value: Groups.Operations

data.name: Kustomize.Title
data.value: Kustomize

data.name: Kustomize.Block01
data.value: Kustomize composes and customizes Kubernetes manifests without requiring a template language. A common layout has a reusable base and environment-specific overlays such as development, staging, and production.

data.name: Kustomize.Group
data.value: Groups.Operations

data.name: ArgoCdEGitops.Title
data.value: Argo CD and GitOps

data.name: ArgoCdEGitops.Block01
data.value: GitOps treats a version-controlled repository as a source of desired configuration. Argo CD compares repository state with cluster state and reconciles differences according to its configuration. The visualizer displays resources; it does not perform GitOps synchronization.

data.name: ArgoCdEGitops.Group
data.value: Groups.Operations

data.name: Observabilidade.Title
data.value: Observability

data.name: Observabilidade.Block01
data.value: Observability combines logs, metrics, traces, and events to understand system behavior. Kubernetes events describe notable object and control-plane activity; application logs describe process output. Metrics and traces require their own collection systems.

data.name: Observabilidade.Group
data.value: Groups.Operations

data.name: ComoOsConceitosSeRelacionam.Title
data.value: How the concepts fit together

data.name: ComoOsConceitosSeRelacionam.Block01
data.value: Workloads create and manage Pods. Services select Pods to provide stable networking. Ingress or Gateway routes traffic to Services. Pods consume configuration and storage; policies constrain their access; schedulers place them on Nodes. These links have different meanings and should not all be read as ownership.

data.name: ComoOsConceitosSeRelacionam.Group
data.value: Groups.Architecture

data.name: HierarquiaMentalRecomendada.Title
data.value: A useful mental model

data.name: HierarquiaMentalRecomendada.Block01
data.value: Start with structural ownership: a Deployment owns ReplicaSets, and ReplicaSets own Pods. Then add other relationships: Services select Pods; routes point to Services; Pods reference configuration, identities, and claims; policies select workloads. Shared labels can help visualize an association, but a label match alone does not prove that one resource depends on another.

data.name: HierarquiaMentalRecomendada.Group
data.value: Groups.Architecture

data.name: ArquiteturaDeUmaAplicacaoTipica.Title
data.value: A typical application architecture

data.name: ArquiteturaDeUmaAplicacaoTipica.Block01
data.value: A .NET application might use a Gateway or Ingress to route requests to an API Service. That Service selects API Pods managed by a Deployment. The Pods consume ConfigMaps and Secrets, mount a PVC, and connect to a database Service backed by a StatefulSet and persistent storage. An HPA can adjust the Deployment's replica count, while a PDB limits voluntary disruption.

data.name: ArquiteturaDeUmaAplicacaoTipica.Group
data.value: Groups.Architecture

data.name: ResumoFinal.Title
data.value: Summary

data.name: ResumoFinal.Block02
data.value: Keep the distinction between structure and relationships: Cluster is the broadest context; Nodes and Namespaces belong to it; workloads in Namespaces create Pods; Pods run Containers. Many other resources point to, select, configure, or constrain these objects rather than forming ownership hierarchy.

data.name: ResumoFinal.Group
data.value: Groups.Architecture

data.name: Practical.DeploymentStatefulsetDaemonset.Title
data.value: Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet

data.name: Practical.DeploymentStatefulsetDaemonset.Block01
data.value: Use a Deployment for interchangeable replicas. StatefulSet provides ordinal identity and can create one PVC per replica; it does not replicate data or make an application highly available by itself. DaemonSet runs on each eligible Node. Use Job for finite work and CronJob to create Jobs on a schedule. A ReplicaSet is normally managed by a Deployment.

data.name: Practical.DeploymentStatefulsetDaemonset.Block03
data.value: References: Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, and Jobs.

data.name: Practical.ServiceIngressGateway.Title
data.value: Service, Ingress, and Gateway API

data.name: Practical.ServiceIngressGateway.Block01
data.value: A Service provides a stable address and selects Pods by labels. Ingress/Gateway define external routes to Services. Ingress needs a controller; its API is frozen, and Kubernetes recommends considering Gateway API for new routing features.

data.name: Practical.ServiceIngressGateway.Block03
data.value: References: Service, Ingress, and Gateway API.

data.name: Practical.ConfigurationIdentityPermissions.Title
data.value: Configuration, identity, and permissions

data.name: Practical.ConfigurationIdentityPermissions.Block01
data.value: A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive settings; a Secret represents sensitive data, but Base64 is not encryption. A ServiceAccount identifies a Pod. Role/ClusterRole define permissions; RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding associate subjects with roles.

data.name: Practical.ConfigurationIdentityPermissions.Block03
data.value: Use fictional credentials in examples. References: ConfigMap, Secret, ServiceAccount, and RBAC.

data.name: Practical.PvcPvStorageclass.Title
data.value: PVC, PV, and StorageClass

data.name: Practical.PvcPvStorageclass.Block01
data.value: Applications request storage with a PVC. The cluster binds the claim to an existing PV or provisions one dynamically according to a StorageClass. Users usually create PVCs; administrators and provisioners manage PVs. Local volumes depend on a specific Node.

data.name: Practical.PvcPvStorageclass.Block03
data.value: References: Persistent Volumes, StorageClass, and dynamic provisioning.

data.name: Practical.ScalingHealthAvailability.Title
data.value: Scaling, health, and availability

data.name: Practical.ScalingHealthAvailability.Block01
data.value: HPA changes replica count based on metrics; VPA recommends or changes per-Pod requests/limits and is usually installed separately; PDB limits voluntary disruptions. Requests/limits and probes configure a container/Pod; they are not controller resources.

data.name: Practical.ScalingHealthAvailability.Block03
data.value: References: HPA, probes, disruptions/PDB, and VPA.

data.name: Practical.PoliciesScheduling.Title
data.value: Policies and scheduling

data.name: Practical.PoliciesScheduling.Block01
data.value: NetworkPolicy selects Pods and requires a plugin that enforces it. ResourceQuota limits namespace totals; LimitRange sets per-object defaults and bounds. PriorityClass affects scheduling priority; affinity, taints/tolerations, and topology spread influence Pod placement.

data.name: Practical.PoliciesScheduling.Block03
data.value: References: NetworkPolicy, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, and scheduling.

data.name: Practical.ExtensibilityDelivery.Title
data.value: Extensibility and delivery

data.name: Practical.ExtensibilityDelivery.Block01
data.value: A CRD adds an API type; a controller/Operator implements its behavior. Helm packages templates, Kustomize composes overlays, and Argo CD reconciles manifests from Git. These tools have different roles and do not replace Deployment/StatefulSet.

data.name: Practical.ExtensibilityDelivery.Block03
data.value: References: Custom Resources/CRD, Helm, Kustomize, and Argo CD.

data.name: Practical.NamespacePodReplicasetLabels.Title
data.value: Namespace, Pod, ReplicaSet, labels, and selectors

data.name: Practical.NamespacePodReplicasetLabels.Block01
data.value: A Namespace separates names and policies; a Pod is the executable unit; a ReplicaSet maintains selected Pods but should usually be managed by a Deployment. Labels are metadata and only affect behavior when a selector uses them.

data.name: Practical.NamespacePodReplicasetLabels.Block02
data.value: Clusters and Nodes appear in the graph, but their creation depends on the distribution and infrastructure provider; there is no portable application manifest to create them in every environment. Check your provider's docs and the Kubernetes Nodes guide.

data.name: Practical.NamespacePodReplicasetLabels.Block04
data.value: References: Namespaces, Pods, ReplicaSets, and labels/selectors.

data.name: Practical.PriorityPlacement.Title
data.value: PriorityClass and placement rules

data.name: Practical.PriorityPlacement.Block01
data.value: PriorityClass ranks Pods relative to each other; it does not reserve capacity. Affinity and topology spread guide or constrain placement; tolerations allow a Pod to tolerate taints without forcing a specific Node.

data.name: Practical.PriorityPlacement.Block03
data.value: References: PriorityClass, Node affinity, and topology spread.

data.name: Practical.PackagingDelivery.Title
data.value: Packaging and delivery commands

data.name: Practical.PackagingDelivery.Block02
data.value: The first command installs/upgrades a release; the second applies a Kustomize overlay; the third reads an already configured Argo CD Application. Review changes before syncing GitOps.

data.name: Groups.PracticalExamples
data.value: Practical examples

data.name: Secret.ExternalIntro
data.value: To keep the source value outside the cluster, use an operator or driver configured with a least-privilege identity. Both require specific permissions in the external provider and the cluster.

data.name: Secret.EsoTitle
data.value: External Secrets Operator

data.name: Secret.EsoText
data.value: ESO reads an external provider and synchronizes values into a Kubernetes Secret. It fits applications that already consume Secrets through environment variables or volumes. It requires the operator, a configured SecretStore/ClusterSecretStore, and controller permissions to create or update the target Secret.

data.name: Secret.CsiTitle
data.value: Secrets Store CSI Driver

data.name: Secret.CsiText
data.value: The CSI driver mounts values as files in a Pod through a SecretProviderClass. It fits applications that read files and policies that aim to avoid an API-server Secret copy. It requires the driver and provider plugin, an authorized Pod identity, and node mount permissions.

data.name: Secret.ChoiceTitle
data.value: Choosing between them

data.name: Secret.ChoiceText
data.value: Use ESO to synchronize into the native Secret model and simplify integration with existing applications. Use CSI to mount files without creating that copy by default. Optional CSI synchronization into Kubernetes Secrets changes this property and should be enabled deliberately. In both cases, limit RBAC and configure encryption at rest; Base64 is not encryption.

data.name: Secret.NativeCompareTitle
data.value: Kubernetes Secret

data.name: Secret.NativeCompareText
data.value: Simpler and broadly integrated. The value passes through the API server and is stored in the cluster; strict RBAC and configured encryption at rest are required.

data.name: Secret.ExternalCompareTitle
data.value: External source (ESO or CSI)

data.name: Secret.ExternalCompareText
data.value: Keeps the external store as the source and integrates provider identity/rotation. It adds cluster components to operate, identity configuration, and a provider dependency.

data.name: HierarquiaMentalRecomendada.Block03
data.value: Start with structural ownership: a Deployment owns ReplicaSets, and ReplicaSets own Pods. Then add other relationships: Services select Pods; routes point to Services; Pods reference configuration, identities, and claims; policies select workloads. Shared labels can help visualize an association, but a label match alone does not prove that one resource depends on another.

An HPA can adjust the Deployment's replica count, while a PDB limits voluntary disruption.

data.name: ResumoFinal.Block01
data.value: Keep the distinction between structure and relationships: Cluster is the broadest context; Nodes and Namespaces belong to it; workloads in Namespaces create Pods; Pods run Containers. Many other resources point to, select, configure, or constrain these objects rather than forming ownership hierarchy.

data.name: ResumoFinal.Block03
data.value: The Wiki's **Practical examples** sections contain fuller translated examples with copy buttons. Names and images below are illustrative; check your cluster's controllers and StorageClasses before applying manifests.

data.name: ResumoFinal.Block04
data.value: Keep the distinction between structure and relationships: Cluster is the broadest context; Nodes and Namespaces belong to it; workloads in Namespaces create Pods; Pods run Containers.

data.name: Deployment.ControllerChain
data.value: You declare the Deployment; the Deployment controller creates and updates ReplicaSets; each ReplicaSet keeps the Pods for its revision running. Normally apply and change the Deployment instead of manually creating its managed ReplicaSets and Pods.

data.name: JobECronjob.ControllerChain
data.value: A CronJob creates a Job for each scheduled run; the Job creates one or more Pods and tracks their completion. For a one-time task, create the Job directly and let it create the Pods.

data.name: Pod.ControllerOwnership
data.value: A Pod created directly has no controller to recreate it if it is removed. Use a Deployment for replaceable replicas, or a CronJob for scheduled work; it creates Jobs, which create Pods.

data.name: Statefulset.ControllerChain
data.value: A StatefulSet creates Pods with stable ordinal identities and, through volumeClaimTemplates, requests one PersistentVolumeClaim per replica. Provisioning can bind each claim to a PersistentVolume; the controller does not create physical storage by itself.

data.name: Daemonset.ControllerChain
data.value: A DaemonSet watches eligible Nodes and maintains one Pod on each. You create the DaemonSet; its controller creates, removes, or replaces those Pods as Nodes and selectors change.

data.name: Cluster.CreationNote
data.value: A cluster is not created with a portable Kubernetes manifest. Create it through the chosen provider or distribution, then use these commands to check the context and available components.

data.name: WorkerNode.CreationNote
data.value: On managed clusters, the provider creates and configures Nodes; do not try to create a Node with a generic manifest. On self-managed clusters, bootstrapping depends on the distribution. These commands inspect existing Nodes.

data.name: Persistentvolume.ExampleNote
data.value: This manifest uses hostPath only to demonstrate a static PersistentVolume in a lab. In production, prefer provisioning suited to the environment through a StorageClass; a PersistentVolume does not create the physical disk.

data.name: HorizontalPodAutoscalerHpa.Prerequisites
data.value: For the CPU metric in this example, install and configure Metrics Server and set CPU requests on containers in the target Pod template. The HPA adjusts the Deployment scale; it does not create Pods directly.

data.name: VerticalPodAutoscalerVpa.Prerequisites
data.value: This resource requires the Vertical Pod Autoscaler components to be installed in the cluster. Off mode only recommends values; modes that apply recommendations may restart Pods. VPA acts on its configured target, such as a Deployment.

data.name: IngressEGatewayApi.GatewayPrerequisite
data.value: The Gateway API requires its CRDs and a compatible controller. The controller operator installs/configures GatewayClass; replace the example name with a GatewayClass available in the cluster. HTTPRoute references an existing Gateway and Service.
